newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader calls for new unity government.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader calls for new unity government.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Sunday dropped his refusal to deal with ex-communists and urged the creation of a national unity government and new elections to help resolve an armed rebellion in the south.

In what was seen as a major concession to the opposition, the right-wing Albanian leader called for an interim government containing all parties, including the main opposition Socialists, heirs to the Communists who ruled this Balkan country for five decades.
In a further move to defuse tension, Berisha also extended by a week an amnesty on rebels to hand in their weapons.

Opposition leaders praised the measure and sought assurances that the president had dropped objections voiced less than 24 hours earlier. Berisha had said the statutes of his Democratic Party barred coalitions with former Communists.
"I meant all parties seated here. It's clear," Berisha said during the meeting, conveyed to Albania's 3.4 million people in a highly unusual television broadcast.
"Last night I was categorical about the Socialist Party. But there are moral considerations...a moral obligation. Sometimes, you have to choose morals over laws."

The head of a European mediation mission on Saturday urged Berisha to prolong a 48-hour amnesty which ran out early on Sunday to give more time for talks and for the surrender thousands of weapons seized by the rebels from army depots.

In Rome, an Italian foreign ministry spokesman said Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was flying to Tirana on Sunday at the invitation of both sides in the Albanian confrontation to discuss with Berisha how to move ahead towards democratic elections.

In the southern Albanian town of Gjirokaster, which fell to the rebels on Saturday, retired army general Agim Gozhita took charge, ordering teenagers to hand in their weapons and vowing to punish looters.

One person was killed and three were wounded during a night of wild celebrations after rebels seized the town, site of the main army base for the region. Army reinforcements flown in to defend it fled to the mountains.

"There will be no more shootings. Children under 18 should not carry weapons. Shops will open and those caught stealing will be punished," Gozhita told a crowd of 1,500 after he was elected president of the town's 15-member rebel council.
But he also sent an unwelcome message to Berisha, rejecting any amnesty to surrender weapons unless it involved the president's resignation.

Rebels accuse the Albanian leader of standing by while thousands of Albanians lost their life savings in fraudulent pyramid investment that collapsed in January, sparking the initial unrest that turned into an anti-government uprising.
In other southern towns still under government controlno major incidents were reported by residents reached by telephone, but the mood was described as tense and most people were staying indoors.
In the town of Ballsh, 120 kms (75 miles) south of Tirana, journalists reported four government tanks drawn up around the country's main oil refinery built by the Chinese.
In his broadcast remarks, Berisha urged the formation of a "government of national reconciliation" and proposed new elections within two months.
Opposition parties had rejected an earlier proposal by the president to hold the polls within 45 days, saying it would be impossible to stage them under emergency rule introduced last week.
Berisha also urged the Socialists to end their boycott of parliament and take up the handful of seats they won in last May's election, criticised by western observers as unfair.
